questions.stem: Andre Walters, a manager at a Kingston printing firm, is asked to research possible new business opportunities. What should he do first?
options: Buy equipment for the most popular idea he has heard
Agree the research aims, scope, budget and deadline
Send a survey to every customer on the database
Ask a competitor what new services it is planning

questions.stem: Why should research into business opportunities start from the firm's own goals and capabilities?
options: So that the firm looks only at its rivals' ideas
So that no outside data needs to be collected
So that the research can be finished in one day
So the ideas found suit the firm

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of using published information before carrying out a survey?

options: The opportunity has no value and should be dropped

questions.stem: A firm has the resources to follow only one of two opportunities. What does "opportunity cost" mean here?
options: The money spent on researching both ideas
The cost of the cheaper of the two ideas

options: Open the new business the same afternoon

options: The colour of rival quarries' trucks

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names research that uses information already published, carried out at a desk rather than in the field?
A town has 20,000 adults. Research suggests 15% would join a new gym, each paying J$5,000 a month. What is the estimated monthly market, in J$?
What one-word term names a small, specialised part of a market that larger firms tend to ignore?
What one-word term names Jamaicans and people of Jamaican descent living overseas, often researched as a market for Jamaican goods?
What one-word term describes research data in words, such as opinions from interviews, rather than in numbers?
An opportunity scores 7 for demand (weight 60%) and 9 for profit (weight 40%). What is its weighted score out of 10?
A market grew from J$200 million to J$230 million in a year. What was the growth rate, as a percentage?
What is the printed or online set of fixed questions used to collect answers in a survey called?
What one-word term names a different product that meets the same customer need, such as a bus ride instead of a taxi?
A researcher wants replies from 10% of the 3,500 registered taxi operators in a parish. How many replies does she need?
Research shows that 400 customers spent J$1,800,000 in total at a rival's shop last month. What was the average spend per customer, in J$?
What one-word term describes regular rises and falls in demand at the same times each year?
What two-word term names the careful checking of the facts, finances and legal position of an opportunity, such as buying an existing business, before committing to it?
Research finds 5,000 likely buyers in a town, and the firm expects to win 8% of them in its first year. How many customers is that?
What one-word term names a rival business that offers similar goods or services to the same customers?

essays.stem: A hotel group in Montego Bay asks you to research ways to earn income from a large piece of land it does not use. Prepare a research plan, covering the aims, the information needed, the sources and methods, the timetable and the budget.
essays.modelAnswer: The aim would be to identify and compare at least three ways to earn income from the land and recommend which deserve a full feasibility study, within eight weeks. I would agree with the owners their goals, how much they are willing to invest and any limits, such as keeping the land for future building. The information needed would include the land's size, access, zoning and services; demand from guests, residents and businesses for uses such as a farm supplying the kitchens, an events venue, sports facilities or rented storage; competing facilities nearby; legal and planning requirements; and rough costs and income. Sources would include the hotel's own guest and booking data, published tourism and population statistics, the parish council's planning office, and trade associations. Field research would include interviews with event planners and farmers and a short survey of guests. The timetable would be two weeks of desk research, three weeks of field research, two weeks of analysis and one week for the report. The budget would cover staff time, survey costs, travel and professional advice, kept within a figure agreed in advance, perhaps J$500,000.
markingPoints: Sets clear research aims linked to the owners' goals and limits
Lists the information needed, including demand, competition, legal and cost points
Names suitable desk and field sources and methods
Gives a realistic timetable with stages
Sets an agreed budget for the research

essays.stem: Explain how you would judge whether the information sources you use when researching a business opportunity are reliable.
essays.modelAnswer: I would ask five questions of each source. First, who produced it, and do they have the expertise and independence to be trusted? Official statistics from the national statistics office or a central bank are usually more reliable than an anonymous website. Second, why was it produced? A report by a group that lobbies for a sector, or a supplier selling equipment, may present figures in its own favour. Third, how up to date is it? Markets such as mobile payments change quickly, so data more than a few years old may mislead. Fourth, how was the information gathered? I would check the sample size, who was asked, and whether the method is explained. A survey of fifty people at one mall cannot speak for a whole parish. Fifth, does it agree with other sources? Where several independent sources give similar figures, I can rely on them more; where they differ, I would compare their methods and use a range. I would record each source, its date and my rating of its reliability in a source log, and make clear in the report which findings rest on weaker evidence.
markingPoints: Considers the author's expertise and independence
Considers the purpose and possible bias of the source
Considers how current the information is
Considers the method and sample used
Cross-checks with other sources and records reliability in a log

essays.stem: A firm is researching an opportunity to run school bus transport in a town with 4,000 secondary school students. Research suggests 30% would use the service, paying J$6,000 a month for 10 months of the school year. Estimate the yearly market, then explain the limits of the estimate and how you would improve it.
essays.modelAnswer: If 30% of 4,000 students use the service, that is 1,200 students. At J$6,000 a month each, the monthly market is J$7,200,000. Over 10 school months, the yearly market is J$72,000,000. This is only an estimate of the total market, not of the firm's own sales, because existing taxis, buses and parents' cars will keep part of it. The 30% figure may come from stated intentions in a survey, and people often say they will use a service more readily than they actually do. The price of J$6,000 may be too high for some families, and the number of students may change if a new school opens or rules on transport change. To improve the estimate, I would check the student numbers with the schools and the education ministry's data, test the price with a larger and more representative sample of parents, and study how many students use the current transport and what they pay. I would then show a range, for example a low, middle and high case, and estimate a realistic share for the firm, such as 20% to 30% of the market.
markingPoints: Calculates 1,200 students and J$7,200,000 a month
Calculates the yearly market correctly as J$72,000,000
Explains that the total market is not the firm's own sales
Explains limits such as overstated intentions, price and changing numbers
Suggests sound ways to improve the estimate, including a range and a realistic share

essays.stem: Describe how you would research the external environment for an opportunity to open a fruit-processing plant in St Elizabeth, naming the kinds of source you would use for each factor.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use the PESTLE headings to make sure nothing is missed. For political factors, I would look at government policy on agriculture and agro-processing, incentives and trade agreements, using ministry announcements and the investment promotion agency. For economic factors, I would research exchange rates, interest rates, energy costs and household spending, using central bank reports and official statistics, because imported equipment and packaging are priced in foreign currency. For social factors, I would study eating habits, demand for local and healthy products, and the availability of workers in the area, from statistics and interviews with farmers' groups. For technological factors, I would research processing and packaging equipment, cold storage and online selling, using suppliers, trade fairs and industry publications. For legal factors, I would find out the licences, food safety standards, labelling rules and export requirements, by speaking with the relevant regulators and a legal adviser. For environmental factors, I would research water supply, drought risk, hurricanes and the handling of waste, using planning and environmental agencies and weather records. I would record each finding with its source and date, and note whether it is an opportunity or a threat.
markingPoints: Uses a structured framework such as PESTLE
Identifies relevant political and economic factors with suitable sources
Identifies relevant social and technological factors with suitable sources
Identifies relevant legal and environmental factors with suitable sources
Records findings with sources and classes them as opportunities or threats

essays.stem: Explain what you would find out about competitors when researching a business opportunity, and how you would do so ethically.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first list the direct competitors, who sell the same product to the same customers, and the indirect ones, who offer a substitute. For each, I would find out what they sell, their prices, location and opening hours, how they reach customers, their apparent size and number of staff, and how long they have been trading. I would look at what customers say about them, which shows their strengths and weaknesses and any needs they leave unmet. I would also look for signs of change, such as a rival expanding or closing, and for barriers that make it hard for a new firm to enter. To research ethically, I would use public information: their websites and social media, published price lists and advertisements, company registry records, trade directories and online reviews. I could visit their premises or buy their product as an ordinary customer and talk to customers and suppliers in general terms. I would not pose as someone else to obtain private information, pay their staff for secrets, or use confidential documents. I would summarise the findings in a competitor table and note what gap, if any, the opportunity could fill.
markingPoints: Identifies direct and indirect competitors
Lists the key information to collect about each competitor
Uses customer views to find strengths, weaknesses and unmet needs
Uses ethical, public sources and methods
States clearly what must not be done and summarises findings to identify a gap

essays.stem: Describe how you would research the needs of possible customers for a home-care service for elderly people in Mandeville.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by defining the possible customers: elderly people who need help at home, and the family members, often living in Kingston or overseas, who may arrange and pay for the care. Desk research would give the number of older people in the area from official statistics, and information on existing care services, prices and gaps from directories and health agencies. I would then carry out field research. In-depth interviews with ten to fifteen families would explore what help they need, such as personal care, meals, medication reminders or transport to appointments, how they choose a provider, and what they worry about, especially trust and safety. A short questionnaire to a larger sample, through churches, clinics and community groups, would measure how common these needs are and what people would pay. I would interview doctors, nurses and pharmacists, who see the needs of older people every day. All participants would give informed consent, and personal details would be kept secure under the data protection law. I would analyse the findings to build customer profiles, list the most important needs and price ranges, and report clearly how strong the evidence is.
markingPoints: Identifies both the users and the people who pay or decide
Uses desk research to size the group and study existing services
Uses suitable field methods, such as interviews and a questionnaire
Gathers views from professionals who know the needs
Respects consent and data protection, and analyses findings into profiles and needs

essays.stem: Explain how a weighted scoring method can be used to compare several business opportunities, and evaluate its strengths and weaknesses.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the team agrees the criteria that matter most to the firm, such as size of demand, expected profit, start-up cost, fit with the firm's skills and level of risk. Each criterion is given a weight that reflects its importance, with the weights adding up to 100%. Each opportunity is then scored on each criterion, for example out of 10, using the research findings. Each score is multiplied by its weight and the results are added to give a total, so that the opportunities can be ranked. The method has clear strengths. It makes the team agree what matters before looking at the options, it is easy to explain to a board, it uses the research in a structured way, and it reduces the risk that a manager's favourite idea is chosen without evidence. Its weaknesses are that weights and scores still involve judgement, so a biased scorer can produce the result they want. Small differences in totals may not be meaningful, and a fatal flaw, such as an illegal activity or an unaffordable cost, can be hidden by high scores elsewhere. It should be used with screening rules, more than one scorer and a discussion of the evidence.
markingPoints: Explains choosing criteria and weights that total 100%
Explains scoring, multiplying by weights and ranking
Gives strengths such as structure, transparency and less bias
Gives weaknesses such as judgement in scores and hidden fatal flaws
Suggests safeguards such as screening rules and several scorers

essays.stem: Describe the legal and regulatory matters you would research before recommending an opportunity to start a minibus tour service for visitors, and say where you would get reliable information.
essays.modelAnswer: I would research how the business must be set up and registered, for example as a company under company law, and its tax registration, including whether it must charge GCT at the current rate. I would find out what licences are needed to carry passengers for hire and to operate tours for visitors, including any requirements for vehicles, drivers and insurance, and whether tour guides must be trained or approved. I would check the rules on public liability and passenger insurance. If the firm will employ drivers and guides, I would research the duties of employers under employment law and the statutory deductions from pay. I would look at the rules on using a trading name and on protecting it as a trade mark, and the consumer protection rules on advertising and bookings. If the business will collect customers' personal data, the data protection law applies. For reliable information I would go to the government agencies that issue the licences and registrations, the tourism regulator, the tax authority and the companies office, read their published guidance, and confirm my findings with an attorney and an accountant before making a recommendation.
markingPoints: Covers business registration and tax registration
Covers licences for passenger transport and tours, with insurance
Covers employment duties if staff are employed
Covers trading name, consumer protection and data protection
Names reliable sources: the official agencies and professional advisers

essays.stem: Outline how you would structure a report to the board on the results of your research into new business opportunities, and explain what each section should do.
essays.modelAnswer: The report would open with an executive summary of one page, giving the purpose of the research, the opportunities found, the main findings and the recommendation, so that busy board members can grasp the case quickly. An introduction would then set out the aims, scope and limits agreed at the start. A methods section would explain the desk and field research done, the sources used and how reliable they are, so that the board can judge the strength of the evidence. The findings section would present, for each opportunity, the market size and trends, customer needs, competitors, legal requirements, the resources needed and the main risks, using clear tables and charts. A comparison section would show how the opportunities were screened and scored against agreed criteria. The conclusions would state what the evidence shows, including any gaps or uncertainty, without overstating it. The recommendations would say which opportunity should go forward to a full feasibility study or business plan, what more research is needed, the likely cost and who should do it. Appendices would hold the questionnaire, the source log and detailed data. The report would use plain language and explain any technical terms.
markingPoints: Opens with an executive summary of findings and recommendation
Explains aims, scope and methods, including reliability of sources
Presents findings for each opportunity clearly with tables or charts
Shows how opportunities were compared and states conclusions with uncertainty
Gives specific recommendations for next steps and puts detail in appendices

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can make researching business opportunities part of the firm's normal routine, and evaluate the benefits of doing so.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager can set up a simple scanning system. Named staff would watch particular sources: official statistics and central bank reports for economic trends, government announcements for new policies and incentives, trade publications and fairs for new products and technology, and customer complaints and requests for unmet needs. Sales staff and drivers, who talk to customers every day, could record ideas in a shared log. Once a month the management team would review the log, look for patterns, and choose one or two ideas to research further. Once a year, a fuller PESTLE and SWOT review would be done as part of planning. Ideas would be screened with agreed criteria so that time is not wasted on weak ones. The benefits are that the firm spots opportunities early, before competitors do, and sees threats in time to respond. It builds a store of evidence, so that decisions are faster when an opportunity appears, and it involves staff, which raises their interest and brings fresh ideas. The costs are staff time and the risk of chasing too many ideas, so the manager must keep the system simple and focused on the firm's goals.
markingPoints: Assigns named staff to watch defined sources
Captures ideas from customers and frontline staff in a log
Sets regular reviews and screening of ideas
Evaluates benefits such as early warning, faster decisions and staff involvement
Recognises costs and risks and how to keep the system focused

practical1.title: Desk research on a business opportunity and a research brief
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a short request from a made-up firm (for example a Mandeville bakery that wants to supply hotels on the south coast, or a Portmore cleaning firm thinking of serving medical offices) and its goals and budget limit. Using the Centre's computers and any printed sources provided, carry out desk research and produce a research brief of three to four pages. It must contain: the research aims and questions; a source log listing at least eight sources, each with its date and a reliability rating and reason; an estimate of the market size, with the working shown and checked twice; a PESTLE summary; a short list of competitors from public information; and a conclusion saying what is known, what is still uncertain and what field research is needed. Give each member a named role: research lead (sets the aims and questions and assembles the brief), source officer (keeps the source log and rates each source), market analyst (prepares the market size estimate), environment analyst (prepares the PESTLE summary), and competitor researcher (lists competitors from public information only). In a group of four, the research lead also writes the conclusion. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in the brief once for the whole group.
materials: Request from the made-up firm, from the assessor
Computers with internet access, word-processing and spreadsheet software, and a printer
Printed sources provided by the assessor (statistics extracts, articles)
photos: The flipchart with the research aims, questions and roles
The source log on screen with dates and reliability ratings
The market size working, with the second check marked
The finished research brief with its conclusion
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the brief
Research aims and questions are clear and linked to the firm's goals
Sources are relevant, dated and sensibly rated for reliability
Market size estimate is worked correctly and its assumptions are stated
Competitor information comes from public sources only
Conclusion separates what is known from what is uncertain
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only public or assessor-provided information and do not copy text without naming its source
Do not enter personal details on websites or download unknown files
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Research customer needs and legal requirements and brief a panel
practical2.brief: Your group continues researching an opportunity chosen by the assessor (for example a lunch delivery service for offices in New Kingston, or a tour service from the cruise port in Falmouth). Part one: write a short interview guide of six to eight open questions and interview at least six people who play possible customers (other trainees, staff or volunteers who agree), recording their answers without names. Part two: research the licences, registrations and other legal requirements that would apply, using the official guidance provided by the assessor, and list them in a regulatory checklist with the agency responsible for each. Part three: prepare a ten-minute briefing with no more than six slides for a panel (the assessor and one other), stating the customer needs found, the legal requirements, the main risks, and whether the opportunity should go forward to a full feasibility study. Give each member a named role: interview lead (writes the interview guide), interviewer and note-taker (carry out and record the interviews), regulatory researcher (prepares the checklist), and presenter (leads the briefing). In a group of five, two members share the interviews; every member answers at least one panel question. Photograph each stage and hand in the guide, the anonymous notes, the checklist and the slides.
materials: Opportunity description and official guidance extracts from the assessor
Computer with presentation software and a projector or large screen
Notepads, consent cards for interviewees, flipchart and markers
photos: The interview guide with its open questions
An interview in progress (notes and hands only if the person prefers no face)
The summary of customer needs on the flipchart
The slides on screen, including the recommendation slide
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Interview questions are open, neutral and relevant to the opportunity
Asked for consent and kept interview notes anonymous
Regulatory checklist is relevant and names the responsible agency for each item
Briefing links the findings to a clear, justified recommendation
Answered panel questions accurately and admitted what is still unknown
Kept to time and spoke clearly
safety: Ask each interviewee for consent first and do not record names or contact details
